title: How To Help a Senior Dog With Hearing Loss
content:
chendongshan/iStock/Getty Images Plus via Getty Images

Hearing loss is common as people get older, and the same is true for dogs. Whilehearing aids for dogsaren’t common (yet!), there’s still a lot pet parents can do to help senior dogs with hearing loss.

Most dogs adapt remarkably well. With a few adjustments, you can continue to give your aging pup a comfortable, happy life.

Hearing loss is common in senior dogs and typically progresses gradually.

Signs of hearing loss in dogs may include ignoring familiar sounds, becoming easily startled, and not responding to their name.

Veterinarians can perform basic hearing tests and may recommend a BAER test for diagnosis.

Adapting how you communicate can help dogs adjust to hearing loss and maintain a good quality of life.

Is It Normal for Older Dogs To Lose Their Hearing?

Yes, hearing loss is a very common age-related change in senior dogs.

The condition is called presbycusis, which simply means age-related hearing loss. It typically develops during the last third of adog’s expected lifespanand gradually worsens over time. It may or may not lead tocomplete deafness.

Presbycusis generally affects both ears. The ability to hearmid- to high-frequency sounds(a whistle, for example) is usually lost first, but eventually dogs have trouble hearing at all frequencies.

The most common form of presbycusis in dogs involves degeneration of structures within the inner ear, including hair cells and the organ of Corti, which respond to sound vibrations. Age-relatedchangesin the brain may also play a role.

Signs Your Senior Dog Is Losing Their Hearing

Because age-related hearing loss happens slowly, many dogs compensate extremely well at first. As a result, pet parents may think that their dog has suddenly gone deaf, even though the process has been unfolding over months or years.

Common signs include:

Not responding to sounds:Your dog may stop reacting to familiar noises, such asthunderor the garage door opening.

Not responding to sounds:Your dog may stop reacting to familiar noises, such asthunderor the garage door opening.

Not responding to their name or training cues:You may notice your dog no longer turns their head or comes when called. This isn’t stubbornness or “selective hearing”—they genuinely may not hear you.

Not responding to their name or training cues:You may notice your dog no longer turns their head or comes when called. This isn’t stubbornness or “selective hearing”—they genuinely may not hear you.

Behavior changes:Some dogs become more withdrawn or less active due to reduced environmental stimulation. Others can appear nervous,clingy, confused, disoriented, or evenaggressive. Being easily startled, especially when approached from behind, is common.

Behavior changes:Some dogs become more withdrawn or less active due to reduced environmental stimulation. Others can appear nervous,clingy, confused, disoriented, or evenaggressive. Being easily startled, especially when approached from behind, is common.

Lack of ear movement:Dogs typically move their ears toward sounds to better hear them. If your dog’s ears rarely move, they may have hearing loss.

Lack of ear movement:Dogs typically move their ears toward sounds to better hear them. If your dog’s ears rarely move, they may have hearing loss.

Deeper sleep:Your dog may sleep through sounds that once woke them up.

Deeper sleep:Your dog may sleep through sounds that once woke them up.

Barking changes:Some dogs bark less because they no longer hear what used to trigger them. But others might bark more and/or more loudly, maybe because they don’t hear themselves as well as they used to.

Barking changes:Some dogs bark less because they no longer hear what used to trigger them. But others might bark more and/or more loudly, maybe because they don’t hear themselves as well as they used to.

How Do Vets Check for Hearing Loss in Dogs?

Make an appointment with your veterinarian if you think your dog may be losing their hearing.Ear infections,canine cognitive dysfunction, and other health problems can cause symptoms that are similar to those seen with age-related hearing loss in dogs.

Your veterinarian will take a thorough health history and perform a physical exam, including a close look inside your dog’s ears.

They may also perform basic hearing tests, such as clapping their hands while your dog is facing away or using a tuning fork near each ear to observe their response. These tests aren’t perfect, but they can give you an idea if your dog has hearing loss.

The only definitive way to check a dog’s hearing is with aBrainstem Auditory Evoked Response (BAER) test. This painless neurological test measures electrical activity in the brain in response to sound.

It only takes a few minutes, but BAER testing typically requires a referral to a specialty veterinary hospital or veterinary school and is not commonly used in cases when a dog is thought to have age-related hearing loss.

How To Help a Senior Dog Through Hearing Loss

Hearing loss in older dogs can be stressful for both you and your pet. But with a few adjustments, your old dog can still thrive.

1. Adapt Communication

Verbal cues will become less and less effective as your dog’s hearing worsens. If possible, startteaching your dog hand signalsfor important behaviors like “sit,” “stay,” and “come” while they still have some hearing by combining your current spoken cue with a unique hand gesture. But dogs can still learn new hand signals even if they’re completely deaf.

2. Find New Ways To Get Your Dog’s Attention

Deaf dogs can feel vibrations. So if your dog is lying on the floor but isn’t aware of your presence, try stomping your feet.

Collars that deliver a gentle vibration (not a shock!) like theBousnic 3350FT Remote Vibration Dog Training Collarare a great training tool for teaching dogs when to look your way for a hand signal.

3. Avoid Startling Your Dog

Never sneak up on a dog with hearing loss.Startled dogs may injure themselves or be scared enough to bite. Remind visitors, especially children, to only approach when your dog is looking right at them.

Dogs who cannot hear well are at a greater risk of injury, such as beinghit by a car. Keep your dog in a securely fenced yard oron a leashwhen outdoors.

5. Let Your Dog Use Their Other Senses

Provide enrichment with toys that let dogs use their other senses, like thePet Parents Forager Snuffle Mator theKONG Licks Dog Treat Dispensers Toy.

Talk to your veterinarian if your dog seems to be struggling to adapt to their hearing loss. Onesmall studypoints to a possible link between a dog’s hearing, cognitive function, and quality of life. So the sooner your dog gets the support they need, the better.

title: 5 Tips for Feeding a Senior Dog: How To Support Your Dog’s Nutritional Needs
content:
AlenaPaulus/E+ via Getty Images

As our dogs grow older, their needs change.

Everything fromveterinary checkupsto joint and mobility support to diet will look different from when yoursenior dogwas younger. Nutrition plays a significant role in helping them stay active, comfortable, and healthy.

Senior dogs need adjusted nutrition to support slower metabolism, healthy weight, digestion, and vital organ function.

Choose senior dog food based on the label and AAFCO adequacy statement, not marketing or ingredient order alone.

Prioritize high-quality protein, healthy fats (including omega-3s), balanced fiber, and essential vitamins and minerals.

Supplements may help with joint health, cognition, digestion, and more but should be used cautiously and with veterinary guidance.

Transition to new foods slowly, monitor your dog’s response, and work with your veterinarian to adjust the diet as your dog ages.

1. Understand How Your Senior Dog’s Nutritional Needs Change

The goal isn’t just to feed your dog; it’s to give them the nutrients they need to support their changing body. As metabolism slows down, older dogs burn fewer calories, which increases the risk ofobesityandloss of musclemass.

Aging also affects digestion. Changes in the digestive system may alter stool consistency and make senior dogs more prone to an upset tummy than when they were younger.

Organs like the kidneys, liver, and heart may not work as efficiently as they once did, and a poor diet can accelerate health decline.

While every senior dog is different, most need some adjustments to their diet to help maintain ahealthy weightand muscle tone, reduce inflammation, support mobility, promote a healthy gut, and protect vital organs.

“When choosing a food for a senior dog, it’s important to consider not just the information on the bag or package, but also the overall company, their formulation expertise, manufacturing practices, and quality control procedures,” saysNikki Giovanelli, RVT, BS, ​​​​and nutrition instructor for the Senior Dog Veterinary Certification Program.

Your veterinarian can help you find a diet that fits your dog's health, activity level, and medical conditions.

2. Choose the Best Senior Dog Food Using the Label, Not the Marketing

Many diets are formulated for senior dogs, which can make it difficult to feel confident in your choice. To choose a quality senior dog food, it’s essential to understandhow to read the label.

Before diving into the details, do a bit of research on the company itself—its formulation expertise, quality-control procedures, and manufacturing practices all matter. Here’s how to break down the label.

Start with the guaranteed analysis. This section of the label lists the crude protein, fat, fiber, and moisture content of the food. Keep in mind that these values are listed on an “as fed” basis, meaning they’re influenced by the food’s moisture content.

Next, look at the ingredient list. Ingredients are listed from heaviest to lightest by weight. Though it might seem like a helpful way to compare foods, it’s often not that straightforward.

Pet food companies sometimes use ingredient panels as marketing tools. Because moisture-rich foods weigh more than low-moisture foods, those items appear higher on the list even when they contribute fewer nutrients.

Companies may also “split” ingredients to push them further down the panel, or include very small amounts of trendy ingredients after items like salt so they can advertise them, even though they may or may not be at levels high enough to provide benefits.

Ingredient lists also cannot tell you anything about the quality or digestibility of the ingredients.

In short, use the ingredient panel to understand what’s in the food, not to make assumptions about its overall quality.

Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO)

TheAAFCO Nutrient Statementtells you whether a diet is complete and balanced, and which life stage it’s appropriate for. For most senior dogs, diets labeled for “adult maintenance” are preferable over “all life stages” or “growth.” “All life stages” and puppy formulas tend to have higher mineral content, which may be too much for your senior dog’s kidney and liver.

However, none of the information on the label alone tells you about the food’s safety or true quality. For that, check the company’s website or contact them directly. Ask who formulates their diets, what quality-control procedures they use, whether they own their own manufacturing facilities, and how they evaluate incoming ingredients.

3. Focus on the Key Nutrients Senior Dogs Need Most

Once you’ve found a reputable company and a complete balanced senior diet, take a closer look at the nutrients inside to decide whether it’s a good choice for your senior dog:

Protein: Should be high-quality and easily digestible. Chicken, turkey, salmon, beef, lamb, eggs, and organ meats like heart, liver, and kidney all provide amino acids needed for muscle maintenance.

Protein: Should be high-quality and easily digestible. Chicken, turkey, salmon, beef, lamb, eggs, and organ meats like heart, liver, and kidney all provide amino acids needed for muscle maintenance.

Fat: Healthy fats supply energy and support hormone production, brain and eye function, cell development, immune function, and skin and coat condition.Omega-3 sources:Fish oil, algae oils, and marine oils such asgreen-lipped mussel (EPA and DHA)Omega-6 sources: Poultry fat and oils like corn, sunflower, canola, and safflower (including linoleic acid, an essential fatty acid for dogs)Flaxseed oil and hempseed oilboth supply ALA, a less usable omega-3 fatty acid for dogs that may still be useful for its omega-6 fatty acid contentOther fats(such as lamb fat, beef fat, or coconut oil) may boost palatability and energy density of diets. MCTs (medium-chain triglycerides, a highly purified version of coconut oil) may support heart and brain function.

Fat: Healthy fats supply energy and support hormone production, brain and eye function, cell development, immune function, and skin and coat condition.

Omega-3 sources:Fish oil, algae oils, and marine oils such asgreen-lipped mussel (EPA and DHA)

Omega-3 sources:Fish oil, algae oils, and marine oils such asgreen-lipped mussel (EPA and DHA)

Omega-6 sources: Poultry fat and oils like corn, sunflower, canola, and safflower (including linoleic acid, an essential fatty acid for dogs)

Omega-6 sources: Poultry fat and oils like corn, sunflower, canola, and safflower (including linoleic acid, an essential fatty acid for dogs)

Flaxseed oil and hempseed oilboth supply ALA, a less usable omega-3 fatty acid for dogs that may still be useful for its omega-6 fatty acid content

Flaxseed oil and hempseed oilboth supply ALA, a less usable omega-3 fatty acid for dogs that may still be useful for its omega-6 fatty acid content

Other fats(such as lamb fat, beef fat, or coconut oil) may boost palatability and energy density of diets. MCTs (medium-chain triglycerides, a highly purified version of coconut oil) may support heart and brain function.

Other fats(such as lamb fat, beef fat, or coconut oil) may boost palatability and energy density of diets. MCTs (medium-chain triglycerides, a highly purified version of coconut oil) may support heart and brain function.

Fiber: Supports digestion, bowel regulation, and weight management. Senior dogs benefit from a balanced mix of soluble fiber (beet pulp, chicory root, psyllium husk) and insoluble fiber (cellulose, pea fiber, rice bran). Weight-management diets often have a higher crude-fiber content than other diets.

Fiber: Supports digestion, bowel regulation, and weight management. Senior dogs benefit from a balanced mix of soluble fiber (beet pulp, chicory root, psyllium husk) and insoluble fiber (cellulose, pea fiber, rice bran). Weight-management diets often have a higher crude-fiber content than other diets.

Vitamins and minerals: Support energy metabolism, organ function, immune health, and overall vitality. Essential vitamins for senior dogs include A, D, E, and the B vitamins (B1, B6, B12, niacin, and riboflavin).

Vitamins and minerals: Support energy metabolism, organ function, immune health, and overall vitality. Essential vitamins for senior dogs include A, D, E, and the B vitamins (B1, B6, B12, niacin, and riboflavin).

A well-balanced diet provides the foundation for your senior dog’s health, but specific medical conditions often require targeted nutritional adjustments:

Arthritisor joint disease: Increased omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) plus supplements like glucosamine, chondroitin, collagen, and green-lipped mussel to support joint health and ease inflammation.

Arthritisor joint disease: Increased omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) plus supplements like glucosamine, chondroitin, collagen, and green-lipped mussel to support joint health and ease inflammation.

Kidney disease: Lower protein and phosphorus to reduce the strain on the kidneys.

Kidney disease: Lower protein and phosphorus to reduce the strain on the kidneys.

Heart disease: Reduced sodium to help manage fluid retention.

Heart disease: Reduced sodium to help manage fluid retention.

Diabetes: Higher fiber and lower fat for weight and blood glucose management.

Diabetes: Higher fiber and lower fat for weight and blood glucose management.

Obesity: High-fiber, lower caloric density, and increased nutrient density to support satiety and weight management without malnutrition.

Obesity: High-fiber, lower caloric density, and increased nutrient density to support satiety and weight management without malnutrition.

Liver disease: Lower protein and added antioxidants to support liver function.

Liver disease: Lower protein and added antioxidants to support liver function.

Dental disease: Adjusted kibble size (larger to help clean the teeth or smaller to be easier to chew) and ingredients such as soluble pyrophosphate to clean the teeth.

Dental disease: Adjusted kibble size (larger to help clean the teeth or smaller to be easier to chew) and ingredients such as soluble pyrophosphate to clean the teeth.

Cognitive decline: Increased B vitamins, vitamin E, omega-3 fatty acids, and MCTs to support brain function.

Cognitive decline: Increased B vitamins, vitamin E, omega-3 fatty acids, and MCTs to support brain function.

Many of these nutritional strategies are built into specific commercial or prescription diets designed for senior dogs with health conditions, such asHill’s Prescription Diet j/d Joint Care,Purina Pro Plan Veterinary Diets CC CardioCare, orRoyal Canin Veterinary Diet Adult Satiety Support Weight Management.

You may be debating a few diet choices—some prescription and some over-the-counter. Prescription diets are formulated for specific medical conditions and require a prescription from your veterinarian.

Over-the-counter senior diets support general aging. Your veterinarian can help determine which is best for your dog’s unique needs.

4. Add Supplements Carefully and Only When Needed

Beyond diet, some senior dogs may also benefit from targeted supplements alongside a balanced nutrition plan. Identify your dog’s specific needs—such as joint, heart, or digestive support—and choose reputable brands.

Look for third-party certifications (NASC, USP, NSF) to ensure the product has been tested for quality and consistency. Additionally, review ingredient names and amounts carefully, and be cautious of vague labels, “proprietary blends,” or any supplement that claims to cure a disease.

Chat with your vet about themost common dog supplementsto determine which ones would work best for your pup.

If you are looking for a vet that specializes in senior dog care, check outSenior Dog Veterinary Society's directoryto find one in your area.

Keep in mind: Supplements can interact with medications or they can duplicate nutrients already in the diet. Always check with your veterinarian before adding supplements or changing your pet’s diet.

5. Transition Slowly and Adjust Based on Your Dog’s Response

When you’re ready to start a new diet,introduce it slowly so your senior dog’s system has time to adjust. Follow label instructions for feeding amounts, and make the switch gradually over the course of a week to prevent stomach upset.

Monitor your dog for signs that the new food isn’t a match, including loose stools, excessive gas, constipation, or behavioral changes like excessive licking or itching. If you notice any of these issues during or after transitioning to a new diet, contact your vet.

If your senior dog refuses the new diet, try to determine whether the issue is simply a matter of preference or a medical concern.

For picky eaters, take a little longer to transition from the old diet to the new one and try warming the food or adding low-sodium beef or chicken broth,canned pumpkin, or a small amount of canned dog food such asPurina Pro Plan Bright Mind.

If your dog continues to refuse to eat, consult your veterinarian. Dental pain or other health issues can affect your dog’s appetite, and your veterinarian can help identify safe meal toppers that are appropriate for your dog.

Feeding your senior dog is ultimately about finding the diet and feeding routine that support their changing needs, and adjusting along the way so they can continue to thrive.

title: Senior Dog Care: How to Manage Common Health Issues
content:
cmannphoto/iStock / Getty Images Plus via Getty Images

As our dogs grow oldertheir needs change, sometimes subtly, sometimes in big ways. Maybe your dog takes longer to get up in the morning or seems a bit less eager for long walks.

Just like people,senior dogsface new health challenges that require extra attention, care, and love to keep them comfortable and happy in their golden years.

A dog’s senior status will vary depending on their breed and size.

Twice-yearly vet visits with senior panel bloodwork can help catch issues early.

Common concerns include arthritis, dental disease, cognitive changes, and weight changes.

Small home adjustments, such as orthopedic bedding, traction, and mental enrichment, can greatly improve comfort and quality of life.

When Is a Dog Considered a Senior?

When trying to understandyour dog’s age in human yearsandwhen they are considered a senior, size matters. In general, larger dogs age faster than smaller ones.

For example, small dogs likeYorkiesandChihuahuasare considered seniors around 8 to 10 years of age, while larger dogs, like Great Danes, often reach senior status between 5 to 7 years old.

It’s important to consider more than just age when determining if your dog has reached their senior years. Look for changes in energy, appetite, mobility, and behavior.

Your vet can help you determine what stage your dog is entering and what adjustments might help.

Signs Your Senior Dog Might Be Struggling

As your dog ages, watch for:

Difficulty getting up or walking

Difficulty getting up or walking

Accidents in the house (incontinenceis common and your vet can help you manage it)

Accidents in the house (incontinenceis common and your vet can help you manage it)

Sleeping more (or less)

Sleeping more (or less)

Changes in appetite or thirst

Changes in appetite or thirst

Disorientation,anxiety, and new nighttime restlessness

Disorientation,anxiety, and new nighttime restlessness

Common Senior Dog Health Issues and How to Help

There are a few common senior dog health issues to keep in mind as your dog ages.

Arthritis and Joint Pain

As dogs age, their joints can become stiff or painful because the cartilage that cushions the ends of bones wears down,contributing to arthritis.

This causes the bones to rub against each other, causing pain, inflammation, and reduced mobility.

In addition, reduced joint lubrication,muscle loss, and weakness all contribute to joint wear and reduced joint support, further straining and stiffening the joint.

You may notice a hesitation to jump on the couch or take stairs, slower walks, stiffness after rest, limping, reluctance to be touched, or muscle loss.

To support daily comfort, consider replacing their dog bed with anorthopedic bed. Orthopedic beds provide greater cushioning for joints, and most have a bolster headrest like theFurHaven Plush & Suede Orthopedic Dog Bed, so dogs can easily rest their headsfor extra support.

If your dog is having trouble getting in and out of the car,a dog rampcan make transitions easier on their joints.

Adding adog ramp or dog stairsto the living room couch, and your bed if they sleep with you, can also help them reach their favorite cozy spots without strain.

Adding non-slip rugs or runners and keeping nails trimmed will also help a senior dog get better traction across slickfloors.

If arthritis or joint pain is obvious, speak with your vet about possiblejoint supplementsor medications. Additional medications likegabapentin,amantadine, orAdequanmay be recommended to help with pain.

Vision and Hearing Changes

Many senior dogslose some visionorhearingdue to natural age-related changes, which can make them seem confused or anxious.

You may notice a bluish haze in your dog's eyes, which can affect depth perception and night vision. In most cases, this is not serious, but it is best to have your vet check the eyes forcataracts,glaucoma, or retinal degeneration, which can lead to impaired vision or  blindness.

It’s important to support and comfort a senior dog experiencing vision or hearing loss by keeping the surroundings consistent (e.g., avoid rearranging furniture, keep food and bowls in the same place).

If possible, use touch cues to replace verbal commands (e.g., single tap for "sit" or two taps for "come") and stomp lightly on the floor or tap the bed before touching your dog to avoid startling them.

Use night lights and avoid clutter on the floors to keep pathways safe, and try to keep daily routines for feeding and walking.

Older dogs can experience age-related confusion linked to canine cognitive dysfunction, often referred to as “doggy dementia.” They may:

Have changes in their sleep-wake cycle (waking more often at night)

Have changes in their sleep-wake cycle (waking more often at night)

Forget house training

Forget house training

If you notice these signs, talk to your vet, as other diseases can have similar signs they will want to check for.

Depending on your dog's needs,your vet may recommend a prescription neuroprotective diet specially formulated with antioxidants, such asHill’s Prescription Diet Brain Care + j/d Joint Care Dog Food, omega-3 fatty acids, and other nutrients to protect neurons and maintain brain function.

Medications (such asselegiline) or vet-guided sleep aids (includingmelatonin,trazodone,andgabapentin) may be helpful.

Work with your veterinarian and monitor your dog's response before giving or changing any medications.

You can also trymental enrichment activities(scent games, snuffle mats, orpuzzle feeders) to help keep them mentally engaged.

Dental issuesare common in older dogs and can cause pain,bad breath, and difficulty eating.

Regular dental care (brushing your dog’s teeth), anddental cleanings under anesthesiaare important for keeping your dog comfortable and healthy, even as a senior.

When brushing your dog’s teeth, make sure to use adog-specific toothpaste and toothbrush. You can also offer a dental chew or dental water additives approved by your veterinarian to help slow plaque and tartar build-up.

Just like humans, dogs also need preventative dental cleanings anddental X-rays.  Dental disease and pain can be very subtle and difficult to determine without routine visits to your veterinarian.

Some older dogs gain weight due to slower metabolism, while others lose weight due to muscle loss or health problems.

Ask your vet to assess yourdog’s body condition scoreand adjust their diet to maintain a healthy weight.

Because weight changes can also signal medical issues such ashypothyroidism,kidney disease,diabetes, or dental pain, a checkup is recommended before altering your dog’s diet.

What constitutes the best diet for a senior dog will vary depending on a senior dog's health and disease status.

Senior dog diets can be good options for some seniors, but currently, there is no standardnutrient profilefor what constitutes a senior diet, as it depends on the individual dog.

Seniors can have varying needs, based on their overall health status. Because of this, it is always best to talk to your vet about which diet would be best for your senior.

With age, organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver may not function as efficiently. Routine wellness exams twice a year can help detect problems early.

It’s recommended that screenings always include a physical exam,complete blood count, chemistry panel, andurinalysis.

Depending on your dog’s health, your vet may recommend specific diet changes or medications for underlying health issues.

For example, heart disease in senior dogs may lead to fatigue, coughing, or fluid retention, and is often managed with medications such aspimobendan, along withlow-sodium diets that reduce strain on the heart, likePurina Pro Plan Veterinary Diet CardioCareorHill’s Prescription Diet Heart Care Dog Food.

Kidney disease can cause increased thirst, urination, and weight loss; treatment typically includesprescription renal diets that limit phosphorus while maintaining essential nutrients to slow progression of the disease. Your vet may recommend a prescription diet such asHill’s Kidney Care Dog Food.

Liver issues may result in decreased appetite, vomiting, or jaundice. Dogs can be supported with liver-friendly diets, along with added antioxidants and nutrients to aid liver regeneration and detoxification.

Together, these targeted diets and medications help senior dogs maintain organ function, energy, and quality of life.

Some symptoms are more severe than others in senior dogs.Contact your vet if your dog shows any of the following signs:

Loss of appetiteorvomiting

Loss of appetiteorvomiting

Coughingor labored breathing

Coughingor labored breathing

Increased thirst or urination

Increased thirst or urination

Limpingor difficulty walking (signs ofpain)

Limpingor difficulty walking (signs ofpain)

Disorientation or sudden behavior changes

Disorientation or sudden behavior changes

Sudden hind-end weakness

Sudden hind-end weakness

If you are looking for a vet that specializes in senior dog care, check outSenior Dog Veterinary Society's directoryto find one in your area.

Why Senior Dog Care Matters

Senior dogs have different needs than younger ones. Regular checkups and preventive care help catch problems early, help to ease pain, and improve quality of life.

With the right support, senior dogs can stay active and enjoy their favorite things, whether that’s a daily walk, a cozy nap, or simply time with you.

title: 6 Things To Know About Adopting a Senior Dog
content:
SolStock/E+ via Getty Images

Senior dogsare often overlooked in shelters, compared to younger dogs and puppies.

However, dogs in their golden years have much to offer and can complement your family if simply given the chance.

There are many benefits to choosing a senior pup, and it’s important to consider them during yourdog adoption journey.

Senior dogs are often overlooked in shelters, but their calm temperaments and low energy levels make them ideal companions.

Older dogs are typically housebroken and are still capable of learning new behaviors.

Adopting a senior pup will require preparation, including possibly using mobility aids like dog stairs or a ramp.

Many breed-specific senior rescues will transport pups across state lines.

What Age Is a Dog a Considered a Senior?

In general, “senior” dogs areconsidered 7 years of age or older. More specifically, senior status is 7 years of age formedium- and large-sized dogs.

Becausesmall breedshave longer lifespans, they approachsenior statusaround 11 years of age. However,giant breed dogsare considered seniors when they are around 5 years old, due to their shorter lifespans.

Why You Should Adopt a Senior Dog

Senior Dogs are Often Overlooked

Senior dogs are often overlooked in shelters because most people looking to adopt are searching for anenergetic puppyto take home.

Approximately5.8 million dogs enter U.S. shelters each year, with a large portion being senior dogs. However, only 25% of seniors get adopted compared to 60% for younger dogs and puppies.

People can be more apprehensive about adopting a senior dog for many reasons. For one, senior dogs may come with health issues that need long-term management, which increases the cost for care.

Similarly, because seniors have less life left, pet parents may be nervous about having to consider their quality of life and potential difficult decisions to be made soon after the adoption.

Older dogs can also come with unknown histories, which can cause concern for how they may fit into the family.

It’s important to note that senior dogs still have much to offer in their later years, and providing a safe and loving home could be the ultimate gift from a pet parent.

They Can Still Learn New Tricks

Senior dogs are often already housebroken and well-trained. However, you can still teach an old dog new tricks!

Senior dogs are generally eager and willing to learn, and if they aren’t housebroken,you can still teach them.

Teaching them new skills, such as putting a toy back in the toy bin or pawing a door when they need to go outside, also helps keep their cognitive function sharper and provides a sense of purpose.

Because adoptable dogs often have unknown or incomplete backstories, pet parents should expect an adjustment phase and the need to teach rules or behaviors to fit their household.

They Offer a More Relaxed Environment

Senior dogs are generally calmer and more relaxed due to their older age. Families used to living a more relaxed lifestyle, but who still want to add a canine companion, can benefit from choosing a senior dog.

They Still Have So Much Love to Give

Age is just a number.

Senior dogs are filled with love and deserve to live out their remaining years in a safe, loving home. By choosing to adopt a senior dog, you can provide that second chance to them.

Many dogs in shelters are not yet grown, and theiranticipated height and weightis generally estimated. However, senior dogs are already full-grown, which means pet parents know exactly what to expect.

Their Temperaments Are Known

Pet parents know the dog’s temperament when adopting a senior. Senior dogs also have generally outgrown puppy behaviors, like chewing, so this is less of a concern for potential adopters.

Considerations for Adopting a Senior Dog

When adopting a senior dog, it’s important to schedule a veterinarian visit as soon as you can. This identifies any underlying health conditions early so that any long-term management can be discussed.

Ensuring your home has all the necessary items for your new senior pup makes the transition from the shelter less stressful.

For example, if yoursenior dog has any mobility issues, it’s important to block off stairs with apet gateto keep them safe. Usingdog stairs or a rampcan help your new pup get in and out of a car and up on couches or beds with ease.

Other common senior products that may be helpful to have on hand includesenior dog toyslike aKONG,elevated food bowls, and anorthopedic dog bed. Placing rugs on slippery floors can also help your senior dog walk without slipping.

Generally, monthly preventatives forfleas, ticks, andheartwormsare started while a dog is at the shelter. However, if they are not, you’ll want to immediately start those medications, such asBravectoandInterceptor Plus, to keep your dog protected.

Continueadministering these preventatives year-roundto keep your dog healthy and parasite-free.

How To Find a Senior Dog Near You

To find a senior dog near you, look up local rescues in your area. If you’re looking to adopt a specific breed, such as aGolden Retrieveror aPug, search for breed-specific shelters. Many rescues will even transport dogs across state lines.

You can also visit your local shelter and speak with the staff about any senior dogs who have been recently surrendered and are looking for new homes.

Adopting a Senior Dog FAQs

Where is the best place to get a senior dog?

The best place to get a senior dog is at your local shelter. Many senior pups enter shelters each day, and they have a much lower adoption rate than younger dogs.

Is adopting a senior dog worth it?

Yes! Senior dogs have so much to offer families and if given the chance, they will warm your heart and provide unconditional love.

What is the 3-3-3 rule when adopting a dog?

This rule refers to your dog’s adjustment to their new home. It generally takes dogs three days to initially adjust to your home, followed by around three weeks of bonding and getting used to your lifestyle and daily routine. It then takes about three months for your dog to build trust and really settle in.

title: Does My Dog Need Dog Stairs or a Dog Ramp?
content:
Ирина Мещерякова/iStock/Getty Images Plus via Getty Images

Many products are available today to give your pet a little extra help getting around. Dog ramps and dog stairs are used by many pet parents for this reason, and they have several benefits for your dog’s health and well-being.

It’s important to recognize the signs that your dog may need a little extra assistance getting into and out of cars or onto furniture, so that you can choose a product that best fits your dog’s needs.

Dog stairs and ramps help protect your dog's joints by reducing the strain caused by jumping onto elevated surfaces.

Senior dogs, those with mobility issues, or dogs recovering from surgery can benefit from using stairs or ramps for easier access to furniture or vehicles.

Dog ramps are generally gentler on joints and better for larger dogs or those with arthritis, while stairs may suit smaller, more agile pets.

What are Dog Ramps and Dog Stairs?

Dog ramps and dog stairsare products that give our canine companions accessibility to areas they may not otherwise be able to easily go, such as the car or the couch. These products provide a way for dogs to get from the floor to an elevated surface with relative ease.

Stairs and ramps for dogs have health benefits primarily related to a dog’s joints. These benefits include:

Jumping up and down from elevated surfaces can be damaging to a dog’s joints over time, especially those that havearthritis.

Jumping up and down from elevated surfaces can be damaging to a dog’s joints over time, especially those that havearthritis.

The force of jumping up and down canstrain the ligamentsof the joint as well as wear down the protective coating within the joint, called the cartilage.

The force of jumping up and down canstrain the ligamentsof the joint as well as wear down the protective coating within the joint, called the cartilage.

Over time, this can lead to significantjoint painthat may require veterinary intervention orpain medicationto keep your dog comfortable.

Over time, this can lead to significantjoint painthat may require veterinary intervention orpain medicationto keep your dog comfortable.

In addition to ramps and stairs, pet parents may usea single stepif a dog feels more comfortable with that option. Adog lift harnesscan be another alternative option for providing support to dogs as they navigate stairs in the home or other elevated areas.

Reasons a Dog May Need Dog Stairs or a Dog Ramp

There are several reasons why a dog may need some extra assistance using pet stairs or ramps.

Senior dogsare more likely to need a little extra help in their golden years as their joints age. Getting up and down from elevated areas can cause strain on your dog’s aging joints, which can create pain and interfere with mobility.

If your dog is diagnosed with a health condition, such asintervertebral disc disease(IVDD) orluxating patella, it can be difficult for them to get up and down from beds or other furniture and into and out of cars.

If yourdog undergoes surgeryand is recovering, especially for conditions related totheir hipsor legs, she may need extra help getting around during this time. Dog stairs or a ramp can provide the added support they require.

Dog Ramps vs. Dog Stairs

Dog ramps and dog stairs serve a similar purpose—to allow pets to access their favorite elevated spots with ease.

The difference between the two is that stairs still require a dog to step up and put some strain on their legs and joints, whereas a ramp allows a mild incline that a dog can navigate without impact on their joints. Some additional factors to consider:

Dog stairs vary in the number and depth of steps, the material they are made from, and whether they have padding or non-slip surfaces.

Dog stairs vary in the number and depth of steps, the material they are made from, and whether they have padding or non-slip surfaces.

Dog ramps may becollapsible,foldable, ortelescopingand may contain non-slip material on their surfaces. Products can includedog ramps for a bedorcar ramps.

Dog ramps may becollapsible,foldable, ortelescopingand may contain non-slip material on their surfaces. Products can includedog ramps for a bedorcar ramps.

Dog steps are bulkier products that are not as portable as ramps.

Dog steps are bulkier products that are not as portable as ramps.

Small dogsgenerally do well with stairs, while medium andlarge dogsmay prefer ramps, which are easier on their joints.

Small dogsgenerally do well with stairs, while medium andlarge dogsmay prefer ramps, which are easier on their joints.

If a pet has arthritis or any other pre-existing joint orback conditions, a ramp is recommended over stairs.

If a pet has arthritis or any other pre-existing joint orback conditions, a ramp is recommended over stairs.

Pet parents can ask their veterinarians for recommendations about the best product for their dog, as well as look online for products to discuss at their dog’s next vet appointment. It may take trying out a couple of products to find the one that your dog feels comfortable using.

How to Choose the Right Product for Your Pup

It can be helpful to use a variety of products in different areas of your home to provide your pet with several options to ensure their comfort.

Keep in mind that it can take some time for dogs to get used to using stairs or ramp. Some dogs may feelfrightened or nervousabout trying them out. If one type of product doesn’t work, try another, such as one that has deeper steps or grip pads on the stairs or ramp to prevent sliding.

When choosing a product to use for your dog, it’s important to work with a veterinarian who can provide insight on the benefits and drawbacks of specific products, based on your dog’s unique needs.

Does My Dog Need Dog Stairs or a Dog Ramp FAQs

Do dogs prefer steps or a ramp?

Each dog has unique preferences, so pet parents may need to try a few products before finding the one that works best and helps the pet to feel most comfortable.

What is an alternative to dog ramps?

Alternatives to a dog ramp include either a single step or multiple dog stairs, or a support mobility sling that goes underneath a dog’s belly to assist in reaching elevated areas.

What are the benefits of a dog ramp?

Dog ramps have a mild incline, so they add very little additional strain or impact to a dog’s joints. They are also generally foldable, which makes them more portable compared to dog steps.

Are stairs or a ramp better for dogs?

Each dog has unique needs depending on their current condition. Working with your veterinarian is the best way to decide whether stairs or a ramp are best for your dog.

title: How to Teach Your Dog to Swim
content:
Swimming is an excellent form of exercise for dogs, providing a low-impact, full-body workout that strengthens muscles and improves cardiovascular health. The buoyancy of water reduces stress on joints, too, making it ideal for dogs with mobility issues.

Swimming can also be a bonding experience for pet parents and pups! Time in the water fosters trust, builds a stronger emotional connection, and provides an opportunity for both physical and mental stimulation for the dog (and humans too).

All dogs can learn to swim, including senior pups.

Start with a calm body of water or a pool to begin swimming lessons.

Check water quality first (especially if a natural body of water) to ensure safety.

Invest in a life jacket and water toys to keep your pup engaged during training.

One common myth is that all dogs instinctively know how to swim. While some dogs may have a natural inclination toward swimming, not all dogs are born with this skill.

Breeds with physical characteristics such as webbed paws and water-resistant coats (like mostLabrador Retrievers) are generally better swimmers, and individual temperament and previous experiences also play a role. But retrievers aren’t the only exceptional swimmers!

Other breeds that are well-known for their aquatic athletics include:

Portuguese Water Dog:This breed was historically used for fishing and water rescue; they have webbed paws and a waterproof coat.

Newfoundland:Despite their large size, Newfoundlands are incredibly strong swimmers. They have webbed paws, a thick double coat, and an instinct for water rescue, making them excellent swimmers and lifesavers.

Chesapeake Bay Retriever:Originally bred for retrieving waterfowl, Chesapeake Bay Retrievers have a dense, oily coat that repels water. They are powerful swimmers and are known for their endurance and retrieving abilities in water.

Labrador Retrievers:Labs are well-known for their love of water and natural swimming ability. They have webbed paws and a water-resistant coat, making them excellent swimmers and retrievers.

But if your pup doesn’t have webbed paws or doesn’t know how to swim, it’s important to consider the following when approaching swim lessons for your dog:

Introduce the dog to water gradually and ensure they feel safe and comfortable.

Introduce the dog to water gradually and ensure they feel safe and comfortable.

Start in shallow areas and use positive reinforcement to build confidence. Not all dogs enjoy swimming, so it's essential to respect their preferences and not force them into the water if they show signs of fear or anxiety.

Start in shallow areas and use positive reinforcement to build confidence. Not all dogs enjoy swimming, so it's essential to respect their preferences and not force them into the water if they show signs of fear or anxiety.

Pet parents should always supervise their dogs while swimming, provide appropriate safety measures like adog life jacketif necessary, and be mindful of any potential hazards in the swimming area, such as strong currents or deep water.

Pet parents should always supervise their dogs while swimming, provide appropriate safety measures like adog life jacketif necessary, and be mindful of any potential hazards in the swimming area, such as strong currents or deep water.

Dogs can learn to swim at any age, including senior dogs. In fact, swimming can be especially beneficial to senior dogs who often suffer from uncomfortable joints, includingarthritis.

However, when introducing swimming to a senior dog, there are a few things you’ll need to do a bit differently:

Senior dogs may have physical limitations or health conditions that require a more gradual approach. Start with shallow water and allow the dog to get comfortable at their own pace. Gradually increase the depth and duration of swimming sessions as their confidence and stamina build.

Consider A Life Jacket

Older dogs may experience joint stiffness or muscle weakness, so using a buoyancy aid such as a life jacket can provide additional support and make swimming easier and more enjoyable for them. This ensures their safety and allows them to conserve energy while swimming.

Stick With Regular Breaks

Older dogs may tire more quickly, so provide frequent breaks during swimming sessions to prevent exhaustion. Monitor their energy levels closely and give them plenty of rest and recovery time.

Get The ‘All Clear’ From Your Veterinarian

Consult with your veterinarian before introducing swimming to a senior dog, especially if they have any underlying health concerns or mobility issues. The vet can provide specific guidance and ensure that swimming is safe and appropriate your pup.

How Do You Teach a Dog to Swim?

Teaching a dog to swim involves a gradual and positive approach. Below are some steps to help you introduce your dog to swimming:

Start in a shallow, calm area such as a pool with a gradual entry or a calm lake or pond. Avoid areas with strong currents or rough waves, like the ocean.

Start in a shallow, calm area such as a pool with a gradual entry or a calm lake or pond. Avoid areas with strong currents or rough waves, like the ocean.

Begin by letting your dog explore the water at their own pace. You can usedog treats, floatingdog pool toys, or praise to encourage them to approach the water's edge and dip their paws.

Begin by letting your dog explore the water at their own pace. You can usedog treats, floatingdog pool toys, or praise to encourage them to approach the water's edge and dip their paws.

For dogs who are hesitant or new to swimming, use a gradual entry. Walk with your dog into the water, keeping it shallow at first.Stay close to provide support andreassurance. Consider using adog leashfor dogs that are excitable or easily frightened.

For dogs who are hesitant or new to swimming, use a gradual entry. Walk with your dog into the water, keeping it shallow at first.

Stay close to provide support andreassurance. Consider using adog leashfor dogs that are excitable or easily frightened.

Stay close to provide support andreassurance. Consider using adog leashfor dogs that are excitable or easily frightened.

As your dog becomes more comfortable, gently support their body by placing your hands under their belly or using a buoyancy aid such as a life jacket. This provides them with additional support and confidence in the water.

As your dog becomes more comfortable, gently support their body by placing your hands under their belly or using a buoyancy aid such as a life jacket. This provides them with additional support and confidence in the water.

Usepositive reinforcement techniquessuch as treats, praise, and encouragement to reward your dog for their progress and efforts. This will help associate swimming with a positive experience.

Usepositive reinforcement techniquessuch as treats, praise, and encouragement to reward your dog for their progress and efforts. This will help associate swimming with a positive experience.

Once your dog gains confidence in shallow water, gradually increase the depth. Always monitor their comfort level and offer support as needed.

Once your dog gains confidence in shallow water, gradually increase the depth. Always monitor their comfort level and offer support as needed.

Use your hands or a toy to encourage your dog to paddle their legs and move through the water. Offer praise and rewards for their efforts.

Use your hands or a toy to encourage your dog to paddle their legs and move through the water. Offer praise and rewards for their efforts.

Always supervise your dog while they are swimming. Be aware of their energy levels, monitor for signs of fatigue, and provide rest breaks as needed.Ensure that the swimming area is safe, free from hazards, and easily accessible for your dog to exit the water.

Always supervise your dog while they are swimming. Be aware of their energy levels, monitor for signs of fatigue, and provide rest breaks as needed.

Ensure that the swimming area is safe, free from hazards, and easily accessible for your dog to exit the water.

Ensure that the swimming area is safe, free from hazards, and easily accessible for your dog to exit the water.

Water Safety Tips for Dogs

Pools are typically treated with chemicals like chlorine to maintain water cleanliness. While these chemicals are safe for humans in controlled amounts, they can be irritating to a dog's eyes, nose, and skin.

It's important to ensure that the pool water is properly balanced and the dog's exposureto chemicals is minimized.

In contrast, open bodies of water like lakes or oceans have natural water compositions, but they may contain bacteria, parasites, or other potential hazards.

Before allowing your pup to swim in a natural body of water, check with local public works officials on the water conditions.

Water in the Great Lakes region (including states like Michigan, Ohio, and Wisconsin) as well as Florida and Texas canall experience toxic algae blooms, particularly in stagnant water.

These toxins, produced by cyanobacteria, can be lethal to dogs, who can ingest them by swallowing water or licking their fur after a swim.

Many local authorities provide updates on water conditions, including algae blooms. Avoid bodies of water with visible algae or that appear stagnant, as they can pose a significant risk.

Pools usually have defined entry and exit points, making it easier to control and manage the dog's swimming experience.

They often have steps or ramps for dogs to enter and exit the water safely. In open bodies of water, access points can vary, and some locations may have steep or slippery banks.

Pet parents need to ensure there is safe entry and exit points for their dogs and consider the water conditions, such as currents or waves, which can impact safety.

Distractions and Stimuli

Pools are typically a controlled environment with minimal distractions, providing a more predictable swimming experience for dogs.

Open bodies of water such as lakes or oceans can have various stimuli, including waves, currents, wildlife, and other dogs or people. These additional factors may affect a dog's comfort level, attention, and behavior while swimming.

In a pool, the water is usually clear, allowing both the dog and the pet parent to see each other easily. In open bodies of water, visibility can vary depending on factors like water clarity, waves, or vegetation.

Dogs need to navigate these conditions and rely on their swimming skills and instincts while staying close to their pet parents.

Swimming Accessories for Dogs

When going swimming with your dog, it's important to have a few essentials on hand to ensure their safety, comfort, and enjoyment. Consider bringing:

Safety gear like a life jacket

Safety gear like a life jacket

Dog towelsto dry your pup off after swimming

Dog towelsto dry your pup off after swimming

Fresh water and water bowl. Bring acollapsible dog water bowlor aportable dog water bottlefor easy access

Dog sunscreen(if needed) to protect them from harmful UV rays. Consult with your veterinarian for suitable sunscreen options for your dog

Water toys or floating devices

Leash and collar/harnesswithdog ID tags

Specific items may vary based on the swimming location, your dog's needs, and any specific requirements or regulations of the area.

Be prepared, prioritize your dog's safety, and enjoy your swimming adventure together.

Swimming Lessons for Dogs

Swimming lessons for dogs and group lessons for pet parents are available in many areas.

These lessons are typically offered by professional trainers, swimming facilities, or specialized doggy daycare centers that have swimming facilities.

They can provide guidance on teaching your dog to swim, improving their swimming skills, and ensuring their safety in the water.

Group lessons for pet parents can also be beneficial, as they provide an opportunity to learn alongside other pet parents, share experiences, and receive expert instruction.

Some doggy daycares also offer pool options as part of their services. These facilities may have specially designed swimming pools or access to safe water bodies where dogs can swim and play under supervision.

Doggy daycares with pool options can be a great choice for pet parents who want their dogs to socialize, exercise, and have fun in the water while being supervised by trained staff.

If you're interested in swimming lessons or finding doggy daycares with pool options, search online, consult with local trainers or veterinarians, and inquire with pet businesses in your area to find out what options are available.

title: 6 Best Ear Cleaners for Dogs in 2026, Recommended by Vets
content:
PetMD Vet Advisory Panel

Capuski/E+ via Getty Images

A dog’s ears, just like those of humans, are the ideal home for bacteria and yeast to form due to the ear canal’s warm, moist, and dark environment. This type of environment can make their ears more susceptible to infections.
